utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We shall continue with the evidence of Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Judge, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Oren will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, according to paragraph 59 of your statement, the JSO was stationed in Dubrava prison until October 1998. For how long did they stay there? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed there for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Did you or your OUP have any cooperation with the JSO?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 they were in the open part of the prison. That is to say they were put up at the motel. They were not in the confined area in case something was needed in terms of logistics, if there was a breakdown in the waterworks or something like that. If there was the necessity of having some kind of an intervention. I can mention, for example, in 1998 when one of the pipes leading to Mokra Gora, the mountain up there, broke down. Then, for example, I intervened in order to have this repaired. I called an Albanian and asked him to have this repaired. We didn't have any other contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But did you meet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think just before you continue, I think the answer on page 2, line 1, was that they were not in the open part of the prison. Please continue, Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, maybe that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. They were in the open part of the prison. They were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No need to apologise. It was my mistake. Thank you, Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: During this time did you meet Milorad Ulemek, also known as Legija?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Did you have lunch with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that meeting with Legija?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son who was then -- I can't remember now. In 1998 he was four years old. He had some kind of an allergy or something. The prison doctor was a specialist for that kind of thing and that's why I was there. I took my son there, and I stayed for lunch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: What did you discuss during lunch with Legija?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't only Legija. People from the state security were there. I used to work at the state security. There were some people there who I knew and I didn't even communicate with Legija. He sat at the table and he left. He had some kind of a dog, and he [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] went out to walk the dog. However, my colleagues were there, people I used to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And the JSO?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry because of the transcript. It says I went out to walk the dog.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that is indeed what the interpretation said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is indeed what was said. Please continue, Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And they stayed in the Dubrava prison also in 1999, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Aren't you aware of any allegations about crimes committed by JSO members regarding the Dubrava prison in 1999, in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1999 they were not staying in the territory of the municipality of Istok as far as I know. In 1998 they left the area of the municipality of Istok. That is to say after they had stayed at the motel. That is to say the open part of the Dubrava prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Did other members of state security stay in the Dubrava prison in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not the state security, not the public security, not the military security. There was no one there in 1999. I state that with full responsibility in the area of the Dubrava prison. If you are referring to a longer stay or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Do you know of any short stays by the JSO or state security in Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: I'd then like to call P1996 up in e-court, and it's page 6 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S version. On that page -- now, this is -- for your information, it's minutes from a MUP staff meeting May, 7th May 1999, and in the page in front of you, you see that chief of the SUP in Pec, colonel Borislav Vlahovic is referred to. Now, in the English version it goes to item number 13, close at the end on page 6, and it's the penultimate item in the B/C/S version. It states that: "Around 70 terrorists have been transferred from Pec to Dubrava near Istok and state security members are working with them ..." Do you know which state security members that are being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that within the prison there were one or two members of the DB, the state security who were seconded there, if I can put it that way, to work in the prison. I don't know about anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But could you exclude the possibility that the state security members that are being referred to here are members of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They certainly weren't members of the JSO. These were two colleagues that I used to work with. They were seconded from the DB in Pec. It was their job to be there attached to the Dubrava prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So you're saying these members that are being referred to are only two persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But could you exclude the possibility that there were other members as well that were being referred to here than these two persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot rule out that possibility, but I'm telling you I know that these two men had been seconded there. During one period of time I was supposed to be working there as well where the two of them were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: How then can you exclude the possibility of JSO being present in Dubrava prison in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly would have known if there had been anyone in that territory of mine, in that area of mine, particularly at the prison. You can't really hide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Well, wasn't your chief of the Istok OUP only on paper on this time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of that, I spent many years in both services, so I had friends, acquaintances, contacts. So I certainly would have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 56 of your statement, you say that you took part in the creation of documents that were produced in connection with the so-called Kosovo and Metohija dossier. Could you explain more specifically how you took part in this, which tasks you performed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February 2002, I had this litigation and I won, and I reported for work in Kragujevac to chief Paponjak, because he told me then that all the documentation that was brought in from Istok was supposed to be arranged and categorised because there was an interest expressed by The Hague Tribunal to have dossiers made out of these documents that we compiled there during the course of the war in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But did you draft or compile any of these documents that you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are all documents that I brought from the area of the municipality of Istok on the 14th of June, 1999. I worked there until March when I was sent to do other work in Bujanovac in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Okay. If you didn't draft or compile any of these documents I think I'll move on to just my last question. I see that I used my 15 minutes already. Now, in paragraph 58 of your statement, you say that you read the statement of Sadik Sadiju and you state that there were no police officers from your OUP in the Zablace village on 6 May 1999. However, can you exclude the possibility is that other members of the MUP were present in that village on 6 May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I cannot say anything to you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that in relation to these documents referred to in paragraph 56 of your statement all you did was lift them and remove them when you left at the end of the war, but your statement says that you took part in the creation of the resulting documents for the KiM dossier. You've now told us you didn't do any work in that regard. What is the -- what is the true position?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand me right. These documents that are referred to here were all brought in on the 14th of June, 1999. They were all created down there. When something happened, these documents were created. They were not created in Kragujevac. They were created on the spot the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, that's not possible because they relate in part to dates after you left Kosovo. Just look at your statement and look at the dates to which these documents refer.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the crimes that we were not aware of and that we compiled documents on later, this was done by another group. I then worked on collecting documents and information on kidnapped and missing persons. As for all other incidents there was another group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't move off the subject, please. Just look at your statement and look at paragraph 56 and look at the very first document to which you refer, 6D1534. Now, it's to do with armed clashes between the 1st of January, 1998, and the 1st of June, 2001. What had you to do with that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the documents I brought from the area of the municipality of Istok, that is to say in this period that you have just referred to, I handed them over to the chief of SUP, Radovan Paponjak. As for the other documents that are referred to here up to 2001, it was this other group that worked on that. There was a team that worked on collecting these documents. For the most part this was done by members of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your evidence is that you brought the original documents relating to these events and Paponjak then took control of compiling the statistical results from these documents.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Look now, please, at paragraph 22 of your statement. A very minor matter, I think. The very first date referred to in the English translation is the 15th of May, 1999. Is that the correct date?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information that was received then concerning the killings and abductions of Serbs who had stayed behind, who were down there in the village of Osojani, and those who stayed on after the military and police forces moved --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Just simply the date. Is it the 15th of May or should it be the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it should say the 15th of June rather than 15th of May, because I personally worked on collecting information on the persons who had stayed behind and who got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very short, Your Honour. Thank you for correction in paragraph 22 of the statement of this witness. We just checked. It is 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're getting close to the end. Very often here references are made to investigations. As you worked as a chief of OUP, did you come across the following terms: Investigation and pre-trial proceedings? Could you just tell us what is what?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means collecting information about the perpetrators of crimes, and the investigation about that is carried out by the office of the prosecutor and the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the court take part in the pre-indictment proceedings as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They can give us additional instructions to collect information about the commission of a particular crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked whether -- on page 65, 16, yesterday whether the commission could establish whether there were camps in the territory of your municipality. In how many locations was it claimed that there were some camps? Did this have to do with particular points?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it only had to do with Istok itself, and that is why the commission was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 6621, it was stated yesterday that your policemen arbitrarily entered shops. Did you have instructions to collect goods, material goods, from looted shops?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A dispatch came from the ministry stating that such goods should be collected and stored in particular localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The policemen find a looted store?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They find that. They report it to their officer, and then the officer sets up a team and they go out together with a market inspector and a financial inspector and an inventory is made of the goods and also the name of the owner is stated and then the goods are stored in a particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that place. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department store in Istok. It was empty, so it was at the Istok department store. The vehicles that did not have licence plates that we came across, we stored them at the warehouses of the agricultural cooperative in Istok.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you keep any records about these goods?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the goods, about each and every thing, medicine, any kind of goods. Inventories were made and after that these were handed over to the Municipal Staff for their use. As for vehicles, all the ones that we found, there are records on each and every vehicle and who was in charge. Sometimes we would loan these vehicles to members of the military or to the local organs. All of that have was recorded and all of them were given with receipts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're saying that you actually went into shops which had already been looted and took more goods from them. Is that -- is that the position? Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a policeman would report that a store had been broken into and if the owner was not in the store, in the building, then we would take away the goods and store them at a particular area and then hand that over to the Municipal Staff later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Normally how were these premises broken into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually during the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But by what means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With crowbars, or they would kick their way in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you didn't have a procedure of re-securing the premises once you had found that it had been broken into? You just left it lying open and took the goods away. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We re-secured the premises and sealed them after the on-site is carried out, once a police team comes in and takes photographers and so on. Then if there is no other possibility of securing the premises in another way, then the goods would be stored at the department store in Istok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, sometimes one needs to make an extra effort to understand what a state of war is like. How many policemen did you have in Istok who could do that kind of thing like re-securing premises that had been broken into?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a total of 30 policemen and 3 crime policemen and 1 crime technician throughout the state of war, and also there had to be a duty service, and there had to be operative work, and also there had to be sector work and work on the beat, although it was difficult to carry out sector work because we could not send people out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Realistically, were there possibilities in your assessment to have stores secured by your policemen and to have them since you had these 30 men?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you we had only 30 men, and we often could not re-secure the premises after a crime had been committed. We would record whose shop this was and what was there, and then we'd transfer the goods to premises that we could secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the duty of the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Is this on the same subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the task of the police to secure long-term burglarised businesses?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the job of the police to guard businesses that have been burglarised for a longer time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very fact of a burglary means that we have to invite an on-site investigation team, but if there were no police available, it was not possible to guard the premises. That's why the rule was in the wartime to inventorise and remove the goods and to hand it over to the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier today concerning the presence of RDB in Dubrava prison, you explained who was there as far as the RDB was concerned --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your microphone was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was there at the prison? Which inmates and what did these people from the RDB do?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they were interviewing them, because terrorism was within the purview of the members of the state security sector. They had to interview suspects. It was regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning that commission that inquired into the possible presence of camps in Istok and the findings signed by Djakovic, I should like to ask you -- you told us that you attended your grandfather's funeral. When did you come back?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 1600 hours. The funeral was at 2.00 p.m. Just after the funeral I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you were interviewed around 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't interview me around 6.00. This talk that I had with Djakovic and the others lasted no more than 30 minutes, but I insisted that it all be put on paper, and later it was given to Blagoje Pesic, but the panel did not spend much time with me, no more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you finish that conversation with Pesic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 2200 hours. He was in a hurry, too, because it was not a good idea to go by night to Pristina, and the situation was unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having come to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you've had a confidential communication with the legal staff here, and I take it you've made other counsel aware of the situation. The matter should certainly be raised with the Prosecution if it has not already been raised with them so that we can get a response from them hopefully more or less immediately, and we will happily deal with this as a matter of extreme urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the submission related to the right of the accused to lie. Is that the one? Mr. Petrovic must have submitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. So you're not aware of the terms of this communication?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I probably know about it in principle, but I have to ask the details of Mr. Petrovic during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need. I know. I know. I'll do as you say. But that submission arrived two minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the Prosecution should be notified of this. I think it would be best if you were to make a formal application immediately, and on your question of whether additional material should be obtained from the government, obviously you're willing to try so you should try, but let's see what the -- let's see what the result is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if you do this more or less immediately, we will attend to it immediately, and I anticipate Mr. Hannis would be willing to cooperate with that, but he obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will do during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what we're talking about. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a hard time remembering because it was written five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I know why you wanted six weeks for the final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you now on the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. And we would call Mr. Dragan Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivaljevic, did you -- did you have occasion to give a written statement to the Defence team for Mr. Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I gave a written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: May I have the assistance of the usher. I have a hard copy of 6D1606 which we can also call up on e-court. And as we wait for the same to appear on e-court, sir, and for the hard copy to reach you, I'll first ask you if you can recognise this document as being this written statement that you gave to the Defence team for Mr. Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the written statement that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. I was just waiting for the transcript and the translation. And did you review the same prior to today to see if there were any corrections that needed to be made to it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it, reviewed it, and I should like to make one little correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. If we can turn to -- do you recall the paragraph that you immediate to make a correction to or ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: It is an a paragraph describing how we ran onto a mine from Bradas to Podujevo where Minko Trankovic ran over a mine in his vehicle, I believe. Two policemen got killed and he was seriously wounded. I was wrong only about the time when it happened. I was a couple of days off the mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 of the B/C/S and English page 8. This is in paragraph 32, I believe, sir. If you could look at that. Is that the paragraph that we're talking about for which you have this correction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct. That's the paragraph. 32, it needs to be corrected. Paragraph 29 describes when this vehicle ran over a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And insofar as paragraph 29 describes this incident, would it be fair to say that we can then delete the reference to Mr. Trajkovic in this paragraph, paragraph 32?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I suggest that it should be deleted because I have made the correction, and I withdraw the other part of the statement. The correction goes into 29, and with the correction we have now the correct description, correct in terms of location and time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the correction, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The -- in paragraph 32 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, what's the correction that's been added to paragraph 29?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nothing's being added to 29. 29 depicts the -- the incident and gives the time period because it's -- it's in the -- following paragraph 28 in the time period of March. So the reference to Mr. Trajkovic being in 32 should be deleted as the reference in 29 is the -- is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am not following this. The witness said that he had made a mistake about a date. He was a couple of days out. But in fact he's made a mistake about the event, is it, in which Trajkovic was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the date that -- it did not occur during the action that is depicted in 32, which would be with respect to the date, but we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it happened in a different action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It may not have -- it happened during a different time period. Looking at this, it's talking about a time period at the beginning of the NATO bombings in paragraphs 28 and 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. So can you clarify with the witness in which context Trajkovic was actually injured?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand what happened to him and who else was there at the time at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivaljevic, could you please assist us by giving us some further details regarding the incident in which Mr. Trajkovic was -- was injured, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On an access road overlooking Podujevo town a vehicle was moving, and inside it was Zivko Trajkovic with another policeman who got killed then, it was Aleksic Radovan -- Radovan Aleksic, sorry. The vehicle ran over a mine that was dug into the ground on that part of the road and it was blown up. So on that stretch of the road near Bradas village Zivko Trajkovic was seriously wounded, and that anti-tank mine killed Radovan Aleksic and wounded two policemen. That is the exact description of this incident. There is an error, however, in passage 32 in that we described the same incident but linked it to our return from a certain action. So 32 is not correct. There was a small action in Palatna village, and we thought originally Trajkovic was coming back from that action when he ran over that mine, and that's the only thing we got wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what alteration do you propose then, Mr. Ivetic, that we should make to the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Pardon me. In paragraph 32, I would delete the sentence relating to Mr. Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zivaljevic, apart from the aforementioned correction, does the rest of the text of your statement accurately reflect your knowledge and information about the matters referenced therein?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: There are no other corrections to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now today while you are under oath, if I were to ask you about the same topics that are in your statement would you give the same information and answers as contained in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers to the same questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for the written statement denoted as Exhibit 6D1606 to be admitted subject to the one correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- now, Mr. Zivaljevic, some additional areas I would like to question you about and explore in greater detail. First of all, did you ever have occasion to see any order or decision map signed by the MUP staff in Pristina for any anti-terrorist action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any order or become aware of the existence of any plan on the part of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia for ethnic Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija to be killed, robbed, or forcibly deported from that territory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, as -- as a PJP commander or as a policeman, did you ever have occasion to complete any kind of military academy or school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not graduate from a military academy, and I'm pretty ignorant about military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that regard did you have occasion to complete any school or training of any kind relating to commanding of artillery units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to draft or otherwise prepare any order or decision map for undertaking any anti-terrorist actions in which your forces participated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not qualified for this. I'm a crime [as interpreted] policeman, and I don't know much about this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told by my colleague that at 21, line 6 of the transcript -- there it is, the word crime policeman was put into the transcript. The witness in Serbian said "kriminolog," which we believe means criminologist in English. I don't know if it makes much of a difference for purposes of the subject matter, but we bring that to the Court's an attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is a criminologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A criminologist? We can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you mentioned -- when you stated that you were in Serbian a "kriminolog," which I believe is either a crime policeman or criminologist, could you describe what that -- what that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to describe it briefly. I am a policeman by profession. I did police work, but I also did studies, investigations, and detection of perpetrators of aggravated threat and beginning perpetrators into custody. So my job was to write criminal reports and not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I said I don't think it made much difference in the subject matter but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which gives me an opportunity to ask you another question. In your statement you say you're a graduate of the -- in the English Defectology Faculty. What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a teacher for special needs and a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, did any of your subordinate officers in your PJP brigade ever draft or prepare either written notes or decision maps deciding the assignments for your forces in anti-terrorist actions with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not clear on this and I'd like to ask you a question. What do you mean by teacher for special needs? What is "special needs"? Would you kindly elaborate this "special needs"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Persons who are asocial, persons of asocial behaviour and who need to be reintegrated into society. That's my segment. But in that area, there are many other fields that deal with psychology and other aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there is question there to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will repeat it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did any of your subordinate officers in your PJP brigade ever draft or prepare written orders or decision maps deciding on the assignments of your forces in anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I had no qualified personnel that would deal with that. If necessary, I can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, generally speaking, how did you and your officers cooperate with the command of the army brigade on the terrain in the course of an anti-terrorist action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I always took care to cooperate well with the command because they always assisted me generously on the ground, and whenever I needed an opinion or advice or possibly a suggestion, I tried to accept their advice as to how to best integrate as far as the military aspect was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as far as communication with the VJ commander or commanders during an anti-terrorist action, how was that effectuated by yourself and by your subordinate officers, company, and platoon commanders -- or company commanders, I should say.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed commander of detachment. Within the detachment I had assistants and company commanders. Unfortunately, I had at the most one military officer or somebody who graduated from the military academy. Most often the people were not qualified in terms of waging war or anti-combat -- anti-terrorist combat. Therefore, I relied on military commanders as experts in the field, and I, whenever possible, arranged with them to have my commanders work together with military commanders and act together in order to -- to be successful in that field. I hope I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 30 of your statement, you talk on an anti-terrorist action, I believe, Bajgora, at the end of April 1999. In the course of that action did you personally participate with your unit on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with regards to your unit and that particular action, who planned the tasks and who explained the tasks to you regarding your assignments in this action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to plan or to draft a competent, in the technical sense, plan. I would always receive a plan that had been prepared both in terms of text and symbols. It indicated directions of movements and the units that were to be involved, and I would rely on that plan and act in accordance with the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- now, prior -- now -- now, did you have occasion to meet with VJ commanders before the action, and what was the topic of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Naturally, prior to each action we would meet. The topic would be the planned action, natural. We would agree on the manner to proceed, and we acted in accordance with the plan that I would receive before the action. Even if there were some changes or amendments, they were minor usually, because sometimes the plan did not correspond to the factual situation on the ground, but most often it did correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the course of that meeting who would take the lead in terms of -- in the course of this meeting who took the lead in terms of explaining the assignments and handing out the assignments for the various VJ and MUP units involved in that action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Those were the meetings where participants came, meaning commanders or their deputies who were to participate in the particular action. Since I am not a qualified person, we always had this gentleman's agreement that the military commander was to explain the entire action. I had some difficulties with technical aspects of it when it came to various pieces, weaponry, and so on, so I would always yield to the military commander and have him explain that because he was certainly much more qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to take a moment to show you Exhibit 5D1329, which is a map that has been presented here in these proceedings as if from this Bajgora action. And once you have a chance to review the same on the screen when this comes up in e-court, sir, I would ask you to tell me if the depiction of movements on this map accurately comports to your recollection of the assignments and situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to read this. "Decision of the commander of 211th Armoured Brigade for blocking, defeating, and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the Bajgora sector." Yes, that is consistent, and I see here that in the signature it says: "Approved by Commander General Lazarevic." And in the right corner I see Commander Mihajlo Gergar. If I'm reading it correctly. The letters are a bit small. Yes, this map pertains to that action. I recognise the area, but some details are not consistent with what I remember about the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The lower right quadrant -- the lower right corner of the map where the drawings are located of the troop movements. And I apologise I just lost my transcript for some reason. Sir, looking at this zoomed in portion that allows us to better read the details, does this map comport to your recollection of the situation on the ground and the assignments for the Bajgora action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't recognise villages, and the vicinity on this map, could you zoom in just a bit more so that I can see better and be able to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And maybe just a little bit more. One more.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I will try again. See, the map has certain directions of movement written in and units. I recognise 211th Armoured and 354th. Those are military brigades. And then I see BG211. I'm looking for PJP units which would be my units. Could you scroll down a bit, please. No, to -- up, please. Two companies of 122nd PJP Brigade are drawn on the map, but that is not consistent with my memory this central part, because these PJP forces are too strong, and I don't think that's how it was. And on the left side I'm not sure whether this town here is Kosovska Mitrovica or some other place. You probably can discern this better. Could you please assist me with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- yes. I believe it is. Mitrovica to the left and Vucitrn down towards the bottom of the map if that helps you any, but -- the computer's acting --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I can recognise only the right side of the map. I'm not recognising the left side of the map at all. I don't remember seeing such a map, and I'm afraid that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, in the course of this particular action, the Bajgora action, did you ever act in a command capacity over VJ artillery so as to be able to order or direct them to initiate fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I could not command artillery, nor am I qualified to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the course of this action did you ever actually come into contact with any civilians in undertaking your tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Along this axis I did not come across them, but on this Podujevo axis I was not the only unit. My unit and I never came across any civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Gergar in his testimony 1st of February 2009 [sic] at transcript page 21530, line 22, through 21531, line 9 claim that OUP of Podujevo also actively participated in this action toward Bajgora. Do you agree with this recollection? Or do you have a comment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: According to my recollection, the Podujevo OUP did not have sufficient forces to take part in that, but what I proposed to officers of the Podujevo OUP was to give us guides who knew the area, spoke the language, and could communicate to any civilians that we might encounter. So what I can tell you is that this could only have been a small group, say a company or two of guides, people who were familiar with the area and people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are recorded as saying a company or two of guides. Are you referring -- does that accurately reflect the -- what you said in Serbian or could you describe for us how many -- how many guides would be part of the -- part of your -- of your unit or assigned to your unit and if there were any?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my recollections are not fully accurate, but given that we did not know the area, those were units from Belgrade that had never been in the area before. So we turned to officers in Podujevo asking them to assist us, to give us a guide or two per company. So, for example, a company would be given one or two guides. Sometimes a company did not have a single guide, sometimes it had two. That's what we asked for and what they were able to provide, because they did not have sufficient personnel to be able to assign more people to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could move along to Exhibit 6D709, the -- and I do have a hard copy. It might be easier to hand you a hard copy since it is multiple pages long. And -- thank you. And I would ask you, first of all, to identify if this document is a -- is a VJ or MUP document. Once it comes -- there it is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: The document is clearly that of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could turn to section -- the section in paragraph 5.1 on the assignment of units. And I apologise. I forgot to say the page numbers for both versions. I believe it's the second or third page in B/C/S. I'm about to find it and it ought to be the similar -- it's the -- the second page in B/C/S, and in the English I believe it's the third page. Yes, third page in English. If I could direct you to this paragraph 5.1 and the assignments listed there for the units. Do you recognise your unit in this -- in this list and/or the assigned task and or movement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 5, 5.1 it says 211th Armoured Brigade. That's a military unit. Parts of the brigade together with the 95th VTOd, and one company of 122nd Intervention. I can recognise this company as part of my unit. Then it says territorially of MUP, and then in parenthesis minus 3 and then it says OPG and JSO. I don't know what this stands for. I think that this might be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that this order, and I think that this order pertains to destruction -- defeating, destroying Siptar terrorist forces. I think that a JSO unit did not participate in this action if perhaps we could look at another document to confirm this, but I think that another unit took part not the JSO. But I'm recognising here a military unit, another military unit, part of my unit, and territorial segment of another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recognise the assignment or the line of movement in this -- in this -- in this section as -- does it comport to your memory of the action from Palatna?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to do that without a map since I don't know the area. I don't know these villages. But based on my recollection, I have read before the names of these villages, these peaks. Lukovska Banja, that's at the bottom of the Kopaonik mount towards Podujevo and that should be that direction of movement. I'm recognising that, Lukovska, Banja, Palatna, and Metohija villages. So Lukovska Banja is in the Republic of Serbia. That is the border area. I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you plan out these assignments for your unit as set forth herein?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I realise on the existing task, and based on that task my company commanders and I within the task -- or, rather, I told my company commanders how to act within this task. So I fully relied on this task and acted in accordance with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 14 of this document, that's on the last page in both languages, I believe, or it ought to be on the last page in both languages, and we'll see that it is said that the 211th OKBR or Armoured Brigade I believe is the acronym, is the barer of planning, organisation and implementation of this action. Is that in accord with your recollections from the ground vis-a-vis the pre-action meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 14 it says reports to be forwarded, if that's what you have in mind. This has to do with the military command. They had the wrong regular and interim, and then below it, it says the 211th Armoured Brigade command which is responsible for planning, organising and conducting activities shall organise combined action between the elements of combat disposition [Realtime transcript read in error "disparamilitary"] during the planning, organisation, preparation, and conduct of combat operations in this sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: According to your recollection on the ground was the 211th the bearer - I don't see how it's been translated here - the one organising the combined action between elements of the combat troops -- I don't know, Your Honours, at page 30 line 17 we have -- we have this word despair military groups. I don't know where that comes from I'm looking at the English text right now and it's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you would have to ask the witness to clarify that whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me start by reading it back to you, sir, from the -- from the transcript it says and I now quote from line 14: "And then it says the 211th Armoured Brigade command which is responsible for planning, organising, and conducting activities shall organise combined action between elements of combat disparamilitary groups along the planning -- during the planning, organisation, trips and conduct of combat operations in this sector." Is that in fact what you -- what you said? That is did you utilise the term disparamilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I've never said anything of the sort, paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... paragraph 14 which we have in front us and which I think rather than having you read the text back to us we'll go what's on the screen in everyone in a language they understand. Practically speaking what did this mean on the ground in the course of the action what was your role and what was the role of the commander of the 211th Armoured Brigade that was to -- that was to lead the planning -- or that was to organise plan, et cetera, as set forth in paragraph 14?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: My comment is as follows: Command over police forces was my role. As for planning and joint action and cooperation, we did that altogether. I was unable to plan it, but I took part in it. So according -- or, rather, vis-a-vis the police forces, I had the main role but I had to fit in into the existing plan. Is this to your liking, my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. And who -- who was it that would plan, direct, and organise the -- the implementation of the action, the overall implementation of the action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: As you can see from the heading, the plan was adopted by the military commander. He commanded his forces, and I commanded police forces, and we acted in joint action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you received a -- if you received a written order at the brigade level for this action, this particular action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I did. But if you have the document, could you perhaps refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. If we can first of all focus on one other matter. In his testimony, 1st of February, 2008, page 21535, line 22 through to 21536, line 1, Colonel Gergar stated that he had absolutely no role in planning anything for your unit. Would you agree 100 per cent with this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Not hundred per cent. Naturally I would have been unable to function without him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And whose map did you utilise for this action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to this action, I don't know whether Mr. Gergar and his command drew the map or perhaps it was the Pristina Corps command, but at any rate, I had to adapt to that map, and I acted in accordance with it. If you have it, please show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, do you recall what was drawn on the map? That is to say, were positions and assignments for both VJ and MUP units drawn on the map that you utilised for this action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. That is serious map. In a serious map the units of the army and the police are marked and the directions in which both move.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a moment to look at 5D1414?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this on the same subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You want to complete it then or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, are we -- are we -- I thought today was quarter till?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. My mistake again. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd be more than happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could look at 5D14 -- 1414. And I don't know if -- it's probably best on the screen. The one -- the one I have is not much clearer. There we go. And if we could perhaps zoom in a bit. And this appears to be a map presented as if it relates to the region Palatna.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would this be the type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if -- there is a second page to the document that is actually the second half of the map. That's why I thought maybe I could give a hard copy to the witness so he has the full in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page for the next question, sir. The bottom right of the document has a name and signature. Are you in a position to recognise that name and signature and can you tell us do you know the person listed as preparing this particular map? The lower right of page 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot see it on the screen, but I can see it on this map. In the lower right-hand corner the head of OOPIO, Colonel Radojko Stefanovic. In my view he should be the person who drew this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a moment. This is the -- the exhibit is a map that's cut into two segments. Page 2 ought to be the second segment, the lower half of the map and that's the lower right-hand corner of the second page that we ought to be looking at on the screen. There we go. Would he could zoom in on the lower right of that. I apologise sir if you could continue. You just indicated that in my view he should be the person who drew this map. Could you complete your answer by letting me know if you are familiar with this person that is to say do you know this person that you've identified this person, Colonel Radojko Stefanovic and which organisation he belongs, or what entity he belongs to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think I saw Radojko Stefanovic once when I met him. I could hardly recognise him now. According to this signature, he was the chief, and he was probably in the Pristina Corps of the army. So he's a military officer, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you were able to -- are you in a position to recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could recognise his signature because I used to see that signature. I saw it on a few other maps, but of course right now -- I mean, well, I am not doubting the authenticity of this. It's probably ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at 5D1070. That should be a combat report of the command of the 211th Armoured Brigade. And if I could direct your attention and ask you just to review paragraphs 2.1 and 4(a). There's no need to read them since we have the text in front of us, but if you could review those two paragraphs and comment upon this assessment of the action.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I start giving my comment? Of course you can see that the report was sent to the command of the Pristina Corps. An explanation is provided that the units are primarily engaged in providing support to the MUP and the SAJ. In the previous map I saw JSO, so that is a mistake. It is the SAJ definitely. This is what the report says. In addition to cooperation along this axis, I think that this combat group also created a local route along which the population could move. Later I think that this was a good thing to do, a humane thing to do, because they had the mechanisation in order to carry this out. I have no other comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you -- do you have any reason to doubt or -- strike that. Do you -- does the report accurately reflect the -- the outcome of the action and the manner in which it was undertaken according to your recollections having been a participant in the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is small action which did not require combat readiness at too high a level. We went through the terrain together because there was a spill-over of Siptar terrorists into Serbia in that area, and these local roads were being cut off and mined by the Siptar terrorists. The objective was primarily to free this road, to de-mine the area in order to ensure free movement in that area territorially speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this report is signed by a Colonel -- by Colonel Mihajlo Gergar. Where were you in relation to current Gergar in the course of this action? Where were you located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I always tried to be near him in order to make it possible for us to be together. Well, I mean not together. Together from a professional point of view. That's what I'm saying. So that we could cooperate better within the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me move on to some other matters and I'll try to pick up a few shorter ones as we're getting close to the break, and I don't want to go into a completely new area at that time. Now, if we can look at 5D506 and look at paragraph 3(b) the last two sentences of this document. If I can ask you to review those and tell me what your reaction or commentary is to the matter set forth therein about the PJP and the area of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that this comment, especially the one in the second paragraph is a totally arbitrary one. We had a situation in the town of Podujevo which is an urban area of over 50.000 inhabitants where up to a degree we preserved the stability of the situation. As a matter of fact, two or three times a week we had actions aimed at cooperation. I had a team that would bring milk, cookies, chocolate, and they would take this out into the streets and give it out to young people in order to maintain a good relationship with them, partly for our own safety and partly in order to preserve this urban area. I think that this is unfounded, this comment. I think this is the 354th. I think it is some Radosavljevic person who was not there at all, who was there for a while, but who at that time hardly ever left the premises where he was. I saw him less than Colonel Gergar. I'd like to add another thing in relation to civilians in our humanitarian activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, since you bring it up, at page 18249 through 50 of the transcript, General Lazarevic offered the possible suggestion that the failure of the PJP as far as the Crisis Staff was related to a failure to react in time to efforts undertaken by the army and Crisis Staff to deal with the large number of civilian refugees that were being cared for. What can you add to this -- to this discussion about -- about such a possibility as that and the -- and the insinuation, at least a failure on the part of the PJP failure to act in time. Sir, was there a translation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a translation issue, and I don't know, should I go ahead and ask again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you should ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At page 18249 through 50 of the transcript General Lazarevic offered the possible suggestion that the failure of the PJP as far as the Crisis Staff was related to a failure to react in time to efforts undertaken by the army and Crisis Staff to deal with the large number of civilian refugees that are being cared for. What can you add to this discussion. Your Honours, I don't know I'm not listening to the Serbian translation, but I'm told it's not -- it's not coming through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can the interpreter tell me the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the original document, so the interpreters are interpreting what Mr. Ivetic is reading, and he's reading fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we're being told there's no interpretation coming through. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpretation into B/C/S is audible on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but -- well, let's have our break now and sort this out and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- after the break. Mr. Zivaljevic, we have to break at this stage for half an hour. While we have that break could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. And we will resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. Before the witness comes in. He can come in. We don't have a problem with that. Only one correction for the transcript. On page 31, line 23, the translation was the last sentence: Is this to your liking, my answer. I think that the meaning of that part was completely different. The witness used the word, "zadovoljana." I think that he meant if that answer suffice, not of the likings of somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Now, resume the examination with Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hello again, Mr. Zivaljevic. I'm going to try and simplify my question so as to make it easier to relay to you and to have it answered. We've had various matters raised in these proceedings, including the trial transcript at page 18249 to 50 of General Lazarevic, and we've had other suggestions that we'll get to later that the MUP in the area of Podujevo was not reacting to an assist civilian refugees that were being cared for in Podujevo. Do you agree with this assertion, and can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do not agree. I think that that assertion is quite wrong. We did a great deal of work concerning care for refugees. If necessary, I can comment on this in greater detail. At one moment in the time -- in the town of Podujevo it was very quiet, and of course everything we did we did outside Podujevo, because Podujevo is a town that is near the border with Serbia. The Siptar terrorist forces had for months been digging communication trenches and trenches near Podujevo parallel to the road between Nis and Pristina. We assumed that one day these roads would be closed as well and that citizens and goods, civilians, would not be able to move along that road. In the town of Podujevo, things were quiet. We took part in the normal life of the town. As a matter of fact, we even helped civilians. We tried, as far as children were concerned, not to appear as an armed force that was there involved in any kind of dangerous activity in respect of them. We tried to talk to them, communicate with them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could take a moment to look at 5D436, and for our purposes once this document comes up if I can ask for page 4 of the Serbian and page 5 of the English to come up on the screen. And we're -- I would focus your attention to paragraph 9, which is the last paragraph on the page in the Serbian original. And if I could ask you, sir, to read this paragraph aloud and tell me whether in fact it -- whether in fact you agree that it accurately depicts the situation on the ground in Podujevo insofar as this is a report of the -- of a visit to the 354th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: "In the area of responsibility of the brigade there is no singleness of command. The brigade commander has particularly pointed out dissatisfaction with the conduct of special police units which do not respect the agreed times and axes of the engagement and that the personnel of the PJP is often involved in the looting. Officers and soldiers are very discontented with the MUP units, particularly the PJP as being better equipped with communications equipment and protection equipment than their units, although they perform the same tasks. They point out that the MUP receives their salaries on a more regular basis as well as their daily allowances and that it has ensured periodical rotations of units and rest periods for personnel." May I give my comment with regard to this text?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Rather than commenting I would simply ask you do you agree with the text, especially the allegation that the PJP were regularly engaging in theft?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. On the contrary. We prosecuted such behaviour many times, and whenever we learned of any such things we took serious measures against perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to first of all ask you, we've heard testimony -- I'll strike that. If we could have P1458 put up on the screen. And -- and if I could direct you to the first page on both the Serbian and English, and it's the bottom of the page, the second to last paragraph in the Serbian; and if I can ask to read this paragraph and tell me whether, in fact, based on -- upon your knowledge and experience this accurately reflects the situation as you saw it on the terrain or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the last or the one but last or both paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The second to last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: "The work of mixed check-points of the MUP and the army of Yugoslavia is fraught with numerous problems and unresolved issues since the MUP tolerates criminal activities of its members against the Siptar civilian population - murder, rape, looting, robbery, aggravated theft; particularly conspicuous is the appropriation," probably, "of some goods, technical goods and other moveables."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe the one acronym you couldn't read, MV is translated in English as motor vehicles. Do you accept that that could be -- what that acronym MV stands for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I return to my original question. Having read this paragraph, does it accurately reflect the situation on the ground as you experienced it and had knowledge of it in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a very serious accusation. In order to clarify this situation, I can only say that we in our command prosecuted over 70 cases of abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with this assessment or not, sir? That's all.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I certainly do not agree with this assessment. It is pointless, groundless.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could move along to -- let's see. I've -- I want to go back to the part I skipped before the break. If we could go back to Exhibit 6D709 for a moment. And on the first page -- I believe you still have a hard copy in front of you, sir, of 6D709. That's the Pristina Corps order for the action Palatna. There is some handwriting within a circle on the upper right-hand side -- upper right-hand corner of the first page of this document. Are you able to decipher the same, as I believe it's in Cyrillic. And I --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that what is written here, but I'm not quite sure, I think it says "Mijat," and underneath it sayings "K." Now, is it Lazarevic? I don't know. Perhaps I'm mistaken but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: If that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could zoom in on that portion on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you read it better now, or if you can't read it, just say you can't read it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I see it now. I can read the first word. I think it is "Mijat," but I'm not sure about the second word, what it is that's written there. I see it well, but I cannot interpret it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you -- do you recall what your radio call-sign was in 1999 during the time period of the Palatna action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see it written that way, but it may be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what your radio call-sign was in 1999 around the time of the -- of the ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Lazar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can move to my last topic. Do you recall an action entitled "Drenica 1"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to that action, did you personally participate in the action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, but as far as I recall, my deputy Nikolic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to try and speed things up, did -- yes or no, did -- did this deputy Nikolic report to you after the action was completed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, upon return to my location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did either Nikolic report to you or did anyone from the VJ ever complain to you about the conduct of Nikolic or your unit in the action, particularly that they rejected their assignment or something in that vein? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't even possible. Communications did not work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and when Nikolic returned and reported to you, did he -- did he discuss any problems with the VJ participants in that action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He complained to me about the way he was treated. At one point he was supposed to go there with two companies, however there was a change of plan on the spot. They wanted to assign him to two different axes which was unrealistic. He couldn't do it. And as far as I know, one of the combat groups of the army is simply didn't show up. I believe it was the 37th. If I could -- if I had a document, I could be sure, but I think that could be the reason why this occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... examination for this witness at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zivaljevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Exhibit P1989 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you see, Mr. Zivaljevic, this is a record from a meeting at the ministry staff in Pristina. Did you attend it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I attended few meetings. Let me just check. I attended one meeting of this kind, but I would have to check whether this is the one. Could you show me another page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show him page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Page 4 in Serbian, in the last large paragraph of five lines it says: "The deputy federal Prime Minister took part as well." Do you remember now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attended one meeting at which we presented certain details and problems, and Mr. Sainovic came to that meeting, but as far as I recall, he came to the end of the meeting in time to catch the final words, and I think he stayed a very short time. That's at least my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you recall why he had come, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago, but as far as I remember, he gave a very brief presentation, greeted everyone. But again, as far as I remember, he didn't pay attention to any details. He greeted everyone, wished us luck, and left in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To conclude, did his participation at that meeting have anything to do with the work of the MUP command activities, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me ask you one other thing. In response to a question from my colleague Mr. Ivetic when he showed you a map concerning Bajgora map and Colonel Gergar, I will ask one question, but I will be using a document for the Court maybe to make it easier to follow, it's document P1975, item 13. In paragraph 41 of your statement you stated that you have never heard of or seen a Joint Command, and you have no knowledge of anything of the kind. However, the position of the Prosecution is different, which is nothing you really need to know, but I want to ask you this: You said you looked at the map with Colonel Gergar, you showed him certain things on the map and then you got involved in the action. We're talking about the moment at which you are engaged. You are in command over your units and you say the army was in command of theirs.
