utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, before 1999. Sometime up until the autumn. I cannot say with any certainty, but it was grey camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivaljevic, these were all the questions that I had. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for the time given me. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Zivaljevic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you hold a rank in the MUP in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had the rank of lieutenant colonel, and after that, the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I understood from your statement that you have retired. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: A few months before the new year, that is to say towards the end of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the first things I wanted to ask you about is Exhibit 6D291, which is the dispatch dated 21 March 1999 from General Djordjevic. I don't know if you can see it on your screen. You say this was the dispatch that sent you to Kosovo in 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now I'm going to interpret it. On the 21st of March, that's right, in order to carry out special security-related tasks in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. That's right. That's the dispatch that was decisive in terms of my going to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. On the second page of that document, if we could go to the next page if both B/C/S and English, I have a question about the last paragraph. My English translation says: "The ministry PJP command is to be informed by dispatch of the time of departure, march route, number of employees, et cetera." At that time, sir, who did you understand the ministry PJP command to be? What person would that be or what people would that be in the ministry that was to be informed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that within the ministry there is a police administration, and within the police administration there is a department for PJP that took care of equipment and sending people out on mission. I believe that this dispatch means that this department within the administration should take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't know the names of any of the people in that PJP command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, it's been a long time. I don't know who worked there then. These were personnel who took care of preparations, buses, equipment perhaps, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, weren't you as -- as a commander of one of the detachments being dispatched to Kosovo? Wouldn't you be one of the persons responsible for complying with this requirement to inform the PJP command about the time of departure, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: You see, there are some details in dispatch, and I get my task as a commander to get my unit together and to take them there to the location that was envisaged, and they take care about the way in which this will be done, how they will be sent, and probably in due time they report whether everything went as it should, if that is an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure it is. If we could go back to the first page for you. I mean, this dispatch is addressed to the SUP chiefs and to the commanders of the various detachments that are affected by it and to the Pristina MUP head of staff. So the way I would read that it seems like you as commander of one of those detachments should be reporting, or am I mistaken? Were you a higher level commander then, the commander of the 21st or 22nd detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again multiple questions, and if Mr. Hannis is going to interject his speculation on how he reads documents, I don't think that's proper to have the witness be confronted with that and multiple questions and having to answer. If he breaks it down maybe he can avoid that, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The sum and substance of this is one question, so please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, did you need me to ask you that question again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I answer part of your question now and then if you have more questions -- you see, I worked at the Belgrade SUP. I was chief of a department there within the police administration of the Belgrade SUP. My immediate superior was the chief of SUP of all of Belgrade, and he has the possibility with regard to this dispatch that is being sent from the public security sector and to say to me, "Mr. Zivaljevic, you have to go out on a trip and to take such-and-such a unit there," and I act on those orders. So it is the chief of the SUP of Belgrade who sends me out on mission. And there are some people there who carry out preparations for this sending, and they come from this PJP department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are they the ones who have to report when you -- when you leave, and the number of employees and so on? I think that was Mr. Hannis's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to answer this part of the question as well. In order to go out on mission, it is important to carry out preparations starting with equipment, buses, the sending off of the unit and the unit's arrival on the spot. After that, officers who escorted us on this trip go back to Belgrade on these buses with the exception of what stays in Kosovo, and I assume that they report further whether this task of sending us out was carried out properly or not. If that would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct then where it lists the commanders of the various detachments, is it correct that the 21st and 22nd PJP Detachments were -- were from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the 23rd was from Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then the 35th, 36th and 37th were from Uzice, Kragujevac and Nis in that order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this wasn't the first time that you had been sent to Kosovo with the PJP, was it? I think I understood you to say in your testimony that you had gone in January of 1999 as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. In January 1999, I was in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you get a similar kind of dispatch for that assignment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: A dispatch came always, for every task, except at that time I didn't go to combat missions. I went to other types of missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you -- do you have a copy of that dispatch for your January 1999 tasking or assignment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Allow me a short explanation. That mission has to do with protecting religious and other buildings, Visoki, Decani and other monasteries and securing those areas. I was in only one of the shifts. Before me a number of shifts had rotated. We had a good cooperation there and even two gentlemen from the OSCE were wounded in the area during my stint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to January 1999, did you get sent to Kosovo with the PJP in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Right. I was there in 1998 as well, but back then I was commander of the B variant protecting the territory. I was not commanding the units mentioned in this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when was the first time you went to Kosovo in 1998 with -- with a B detachment, a variant B detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in early July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Two, two and a half months, I think. I can't be precise. I suppose until September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And after that you returned to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't come back to Kosovo until January of 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. In early January I came back to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And during those two and a half months, from July 1998 what were you doing with your B detachment? Where were you during that time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. It was the territory of Klina. We had problems with roads. The main road Pristina-Pec was constantly under blockade. It was not usable. And our organisational task was to keep it open so that this main road linking to major towns in Kosovo could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that time did your unit not engage in any combat activities against the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those were minor combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What you've described to us before, I think, that these were not actions that were the joint actions with the VJ. These were more responses to provocations when you were fired upon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a general rule that the police need not open fire on anyone who did not open fire on them first, but we frequently encountered situations that were problematic, where the police would not move on the road, citizens could not move on the road. There were blockades, ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in 1998 when you were there, you take it you and your unit did not participant in any of these joint anti-terrorist actions that were part of the -- the plan for combatting terrorism in the summer of 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Just one detail. On the road between Pristina and Pec there is a village called Kijevo. It was constantly under blockade by Siptar terrorists. So in one period we left behind one unit that couldn't manage to get out of that village for over a month. At that time we initiated some activities to move along the road to give them supplies and medication. There were all sorts of situations there, women about to give birth, people who were in a difficult state, but we -- for that purpose we initiated an action to create a narrow path to provide them with these supplies, and afterwards with the police we tried to secure that route towards Kijevo to be able to supply them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And wasn't that action to provide some relief towards Kijevo? Wasn't that a joint action with the VJ? Didn't you have some support from the VJ in connection with that action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have support, but we just participated in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Which VJ unit or units were supporting you in connection with that Kijevo action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything specific now, but I know they were from the town of Pec, and from that direction I was active together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of the commander or any VJ personnel that you cooperated with regarding Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe his last name was Jankovic, but I can't be perfectly sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall his rank?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was then lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And your detachment in Kosovo in -- between July and the end of September 1998, what was it called? What number or unit identifier did it have? Was that the 22nd, or was it just called the Belgrade detachment, or did you have a designator at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think there is a little confusion here, because the numbers changed and the name changed. At that time it was called Belgrade, the detachment, and they had the marking B variant when they were guarding the territory. Only later were the 21st and the 22nd Detachment formed. So in total, later when these two detachments were taken together they created 122nd Intervention Unit, and sometimes by mistake people said 121st and 122nd Detachment, but this confusion was used in informal communication, not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We had another witness earlier named Ilic. I think Vladimir Ilic, who was a PJP member. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- well, I had the same sort of conversation with him trying to figure out what the number was and he said the same sort of thing that you did, that the numbers changed and it was somewhat confusing. Were you the -- were you the commander of this B variant unit then in Kosovo in July and August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I was the commander, but we had also a commander who was from SUP Belgrade at the time, Ivan Maksimovic. Vladimir Ilic probably explained that to you as well. And in 1998, in the autumn that changed. Ivan Maksimovic was going to Belgrade. I stayed behind, and we had a transition of duties that did not last long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Approximately when did that happen that you had the transition of duties with Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Early in autumn 1998. That's when the 21st and 22nd Detachment were formed. The commander of the 21st Detachment became Bosko Buha, and Vladimir Ilic was his deputy. I became commander of the 22nd Detachment, and my deputy was Dragan Nikolic. In 1999 these two detachments combined to form 122nd Intervention Brigade, but only on paper, because we always acted separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately when was the 122nd Intervention Brigade created on paper in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Early in 1999. And then I was appointed commander, and Bosko Buha became deputy commander of the 122nd. But the detachments that I described before were the founding blocks of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go back to summer and early autumn 1998 in Kosovo. When your commander of the B variant detachment, I understand from other evidence that the B detachments were seen as territorial units as opposed to manoeuvre units. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. With the proviso that as time went on, that unit consisting of Belgrade policemen who were not trained for these activities, started to gradually fit in and sometimes even participated together with other detachments in certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At the time you were there as a B variant detachment in July, August 1998. Was there another PJP detachment from Belgrade in Kosovo that was a more of a manoeuvre unit, a manoeuvre detachment, an A detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. We had one detachment which later in this version was split into several parts. It was the pivot. In Belgrade we had A police brigade that was trained for basically an anti-riot unit, crowd control, and that unit came to Kosovo and took over these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. This -- this Belgrade a detachment in 1998, who was the commander of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Several commanders had rotated, but it's all perfectly open and clear. In the end Bosko Buha became the commander of that detachment we're talking about. In the meantime, there had been two other commanders that turned up -- turned out not to be quite not up to snuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember their names and when they were in that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: At one point Dragan Milovanovic was in that position. He was there very briefly, then another one after him, followed by Ivan Maksimovic who combined these detachments, because we had the territorial and manoeuvre segments. And finally Bosko Buha and I took over, and from that time on it stabilised a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who served in that position between Dragan Milovanovic and Ivan Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Stojan Petkovic preceded them, late Stojan Petkovic. And after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- you mentioned that there had been a couple of commanders who weren't quite up to snuff. I take it that is referring to Petkovic and Milanovic. What kind of problems did they have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Stojan Petkovic worked for a long time, had health problems, went to Belgrade, and there were some organisational problems, and he was not quite qualified in these military matters. I don't want to say any more about him sitting here. Anyway, he had to go to Belgrade and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and what about Milovanovic? What kind of problems did he have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my personal opinion, I don't think he found his right place in that situation when tensions were heightened. There was a lot of police force that needed to be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, sorry to interrupt my learned friend Mr. Hannis, but for the record the witness said that he was not qualified in these military matters, and that's the reason why, for the most part, they engaged deputies who graduated from military academies. This last bit had not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you first go to Kosovo in July 1998? Do you recall approximately what the date was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be quite sure now, but I believe it was around the 1st of July or around the 30th of June. I can be two days off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you a document. I can hand you a hard copy with the usher's help. This is dated the 22nd of July, 1998. It's Exhibit 6D798, and it purports to be the minutes of a meeting head on that date at the Pristina MUP conference hall. It says all commanders of the PJP detachments attended, as well as General Lukic, General Djordjevic, General Obrad Stevanovic, Goran Radosavljevic and organisation. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I attended one meeting. I'm not quite sure whether this is the one, but if you help me a little at any rate I will tell you the truth. I did attend one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, this one would have been about three weeks after your arrival and it's in Pristina with those persons I named, and you'll see on the agenda item number 3 talks about defining task in the implementation of the -- and I may need some help from my friends across the way because my English translation says "global plan," but I know we've had some discussion about that translation. Can you read item number 3 for us on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: "Identifying tasks related to the implementation of the overall plan and the follow-up task." Related to the answer to this question, at that time, Ivan Maksimovic was my superior, and it's most likely that he attended the meeting, not I. And when he came back, he must have briefed us about what had gone on in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you can't tell us for sure whether or not you attended this meeting. Is that -- is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 11 of your statement, Exhibit 6D1606, you say: "At the beginning of 1998 the security situation in Kosovo became more complex and the terrorism escalated. In relation to this, I know that a general plan for combat against terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was adopted at the highest state level." Now, how did you know about that plan being adopted at the highest state level? How did you first hear about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I heard that from Ivan Maksimovic who was at the meeting. With us, the inner circle, he had a meeting, and he passed on the information and the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say at this highest state level, what did you mean by that, or what did Maksimovic tell you about that? Who does that refer to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose the state leadership, the top state leadership, but I'm not sure. I had no reason to doubt the veracity of what my superior said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you now another exhibit from that summer of 1998. This is Exhibit 6D768. It's dated the 7th of August. And I can hand you a hard copy of this one as well. It's from Sreten Lukic as head of staff to the SUP chiefs and commander of PJP. Did you see this document in 1998 or do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you see it back in 1998 when you were in Kosovo in August?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably. That was when the thing was topical and we were all informed about those documents that we could -- and it relates to work on the ground you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see in paragraph 22 he's talking about the operations that had just been carried out. He says it was noticed that certain police officers in manoeuvre and territorial detachments and members of the reserve force, including officers in those units, behaved highly unprofessionally, and he mentions stealing from houses and stealing vehicles and torching houses. Were you aware of that? Did you see any of that or hear about any of that in July or August 1998 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. In order to combat these activities we organised ourselves, and many policemen were prosecuted in misdemeanour proceedings or criminal proceedings. They were dismissed from work. And we specially organised officers from what we called the section for legality who would monitor police conduct and directly take steps against defenders. And I believe we had over 70 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- cases which we prosecuted in order to combat such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I remember you mentioning that figure earlier today. Is that the total number for the entire time that you were in Kosovo in both 1998 and 1999, that 70 individuals were prosecuted or processed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you now for sure whether 50 was in 1998 and 20 the next year, but I believe a section, it was the section for legality in SUP Belgrade recorded all this and took steps filed misdemeanor reports or criminal reports and proceeded with prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of those 70 could you give us any number or percentage that involved crimes other than property crime? Did any of those involve crimes against life and limb or against civilians involving life or limb?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that report I wrote I already described a number of cases. If you allow me, I can indicate this particular detail. In item 18 of my statement, it says that we made every effort to suppress abuse, and we took into custody certain policemen who had seized or stolen Albanian property.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you -- well, when did you write that report? Was this a summary report at the end of your time there listing all -- all 70 of those cases, or were these periodic reports compiled? What was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: For 1998 there was a report and a separate report probably for 1999, because on the ground we did not have the proper setting to deal with administrative work. We frequently lacked offices and power supply, but at the end, we made a report to reflect the situation. And this section for legality was tasked whenever they were going on weekend leave and were being replaced by another team to file their report with the chief of secretariat and the MUP in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you seen either of those reports since you wrote them back in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw some. In this paragraph that I've mentioned, what I describe here is that the policemen robbed an Albanian family, and we took them into custody, and we took steps against them, which means that we took measures immediately as we received information about some illegal activity. Naturally if conditions permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to switch now to some of your testimony here in court today. At page 22 and 23 Mr. Ivetic was asking you whether any of your subordinate officers in the PJP ever drafted or prepared any written orders or decision maps in connection with your assignments in anti-terrorist actions, and you said no, you had no qualified personnel that would deal with that. Now, I think you also said that you didn't get any written orders or decision maps from your superiors as well as receiving not receiving any from your subordinates, but you and your men did take part in some of those anti-terrorist actions in 1999, right? Joint actions with the VJ? Yeah. You'll have to speak out loud, so we can get it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Joint actions were with the army. We didn't act independently in any action, and our people were not qualified for that; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you must have received these -- some text or maps from somebody, and I think you were asked that question several times, but I'm not sure I ever heard the answer. Who was the person that provided you maps and related text about when and where your detachment, your PJP people, were supposed to go in these actions? Who was the person that you got a document or a map from? I see Mr. Ivetic on his feet, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's in the form of a -- Mr. Hannis is I think mixes two matters together. I don't know whether he has the statement in front of him. I believe that is covered in the statement I don't want to be accused of leading the witness or anything like that but I believe at least one aspect of it is covered very, very precisely in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's become a fairly significant issue, so no doubt it will be a feature in your re-examination. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you answer that question? Can you give us the name of a person or persons who gave you orders with text or map orders for your unit's participation in these joint VJ-MUP anti-terrorist actions in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: This is my explanation: When the conditions allowed, I would stop by the Pristina staff. I had people I knew there, and whenever I could, I would stop by to see them, to make inquiries, to call my family if they had phone lines operational and so on, and whenever there were any activities, they would prepare in envelopes documents for me, and this is how I would take those documents sometimes. And sometimes when I wasn't able to go there myself I would send a courier, and the courier would go to the staff and bring back the envelope that was intended for me for certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And on those occasions when you stopped by the Pristina staff, who was the person? Give me a name or more than one name who gave you the maps and the documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Dusko Adamovic was the person who distributed documents to me when I went there. And if I didn't go there, then I would receive it via the courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The documents that came to you by courier in addition to the text of the order and the map, was there any cover letter or note from anybody at the MUP staff, or was it just the order and the map that you would receive the courier -- I see Mr. Ivetic on his feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Misstates the testimony of the witness, Your Honour. At this point if he's going to do it that way, I have to intervene and say that in the statement it's very clear maps were received from the staff of the MUP, and I don't think that we have anywhere in the evidence here thus far anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be very helpful if the witness would say that in answer to the question, because if you look at the question that was asked, it covers both text, orders, and maps, and he goes on to explain that he -- almost as if he was going to the supermarket for his shopping might pop into the MUP staff office and pick up what was lying around for him. It's such a vague general answer that Mr. Hannis is plainly entitled to explore it further without prompting. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, let me start with this: When you received something in the envelope from the courier, what was in there? Maybe I have assumed too much. What did you get?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Usually there would be a map in the envelope or a decision map or an excerpt of the map pertaining to my task and an order, or if there was a previous order then I would only receive a map or an excerpt of the map or excerpt of the decision without a stamp or a registration number or a cover letter. That was the standard routine. And whenever a courier sent me documents, it would be done in this way, and that was the accepted way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. For that -- that decision map and maybe the text on occasions when you received those in the envelope brought by the courier, was there any other information in or on the envelope about where it came from? Was there a return address or anything indicating who was sending it to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that just for the moment. Where do you get the notion, Mr. Hannis, that there is some text, because the whole of the answer seemed to relate to maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: An excerpt of the map pertaining to my task and order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Task and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which I understood to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're right. It's the way it's phrased. Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So was there any indication in or on the envelope about who was sending this material to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Please, there could have perhaps been an indication of my name in handwriting on the envelope, and then inside it would be stated who drafted it, who was the author, or who wrote the written portion. So this document contained that detail, yes. At one point in time I even made a comment when that was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you said at one point in time you made a comment when that was shown to you, what are you referring to, something while you were testifying here or --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That was earlier today by one of the lawyers over there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about communication with the VJ commanders about anti-terrorist actions. You mention within your detachment, and this is at page 23, line 18 today, you said: "Within the detachment I had assistants and company commanders." Now, how many company commanders did you have in the -- well, in the detachment that you were the commander of in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just be specific enough. There were two detachments, one in Pec with Bosko Buha and one with me. Initially there were supposed to be some 500-and-something people, but we had a lot of wounded, a lot of injured people, a lot of absent people, and usually half of them were busy in the territory, protecting the depth of the territory and our backs, ensuring that nobody would approach us, and then the other half would be in action, and that number varied, of course. Very often we couldn't make up the basic numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you have departed now, have you, you have completed what you had to ask about the way in which these orders were transmitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was finished with that, Your Honour, if you wanted to follow up with something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you said you were shown an example which you confirmed was the form in which you received an order. Can you tell us more about that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these were the documents pertaining to the actions from 1999. I think that they were on the screen and that I explained who was the author and how I had obtained them. Prior to that I explained how we held meetings and how we discussed how we were going to act in an action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I've seen such a document today. Mr. Ivetic, did you place on the screen the sort of document that the witness was describing, one that gives his orders to him for an action?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, here I'm speculating. I believe everything I put on the screen the witness has in front of him. Perhaps he could look through the hard copies and without me directing him have him select what he is making reference to. That's probably the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's difficult to -- to go through all of this statement as we progress, but in the area of paragraph 24 and so on, there is a very general reference to orders, but am I not right in thinking that all the specific information relates to maps or extract maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the statement perhaps. I believe I don't have entire statement in front of me, I have the Serbian version, but I think the one order I showed him was the -- pardon me, the order for Palatna, which is 6D -- one moment, Your Honour. 6D709 was the -- the one order that I showed him, if it's indeed one of the ones that I showed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at 6D709.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see the witness is holding up a document, Your Honour. Maybe he's found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that 6D709? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall have it on the screen in a moment. Now, did you receive that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this sort of thing would -- would come along with a map or a part of a map for your role in the action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you a few questions about the 122nd Intervention Brigade in 1999. As I understand, you were the -- you were the overall commander of the entire brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your deputy was Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Part of the detachment that was in Podujevo. And then the other one, or the 1st detachment was in Pec, which is a city 100 kilometres away. So the Intervention Brigade had two detachments. One was under the command of Bosko Buha, and I commanded the second one, and I was the overall commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The one under Buha in Pec was sometimes referred to as the 21st PJP Detachment in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the one that made up the rest of the 122nd Intervention Brigade was commanded by you, and it was referred to as the 22nd; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were in Podujevo, the Podujevo area.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That seems odd to me, because you're the commander of the whole thing, and you're the commander of the half that's in Podujevo; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: You've understood it well. We were split in two towns, and we didn't really have communication between us, and it wasn't until the end that we had full communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That helps. And the approximate number of men that you had in the 22nd in the Podujevo area in 1999 was how many, 300, 400? Can you give me an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That number varied from 400 to -- 450 to 550 people, because we had problems with people getting wounded and some other problems, and that number constantly varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in -- in Pec, Buha had approximately how many under him in the 21st?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: We split our people approximately into roughly half, in approximately equal parts. So we had a similar number usually. Sometimes I had more, sometimes he had more, but roughly similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Am I correct to say that he had about 450 to 500 as well and between you, you would have had between 900 and a 1.000.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: We seldom had 1.000. We always were below that figure, but roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that better now. Thanks. You were asked a question today at page 27 by Mr. Ivetic: Did you ever act in a command capacity over VJ artillery in order to be able to direct them or initiate fire, and your answer was, "No, I could not command artillery, nor was I qualified to do that." I accept that. I understand that. But although you couldn't command it, when you were engaged in an anti -- a joint anti-terrorist action with the VJ, could you not request artillery support if you needed it? You couldn't command it, but could you ask for it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I could propose that. This is how it was organised in that form. I would ask them or propose that to him, and then he would give a competent technical opinion and would either provide that support or not provide. Sometimes he wouldn't provide it sufficiently, but, you know, we had activities occasionally, not every day. I couldn't order it tom him. I couldn't make the decision by myself, but I could ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it from your answer then it sounds like there were some occasions where you did request it, and sometimes you got it and sometimes you didn't. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. My companies, which were on the ground, commanders of those companies sometimes needed to ask for assistance, and sometimes this assistant -- this assistance could be provided in this way. And since I had communication with the military commander, I would directly talk to him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was my next question. When you said that you would ask them or propose that to him and then he would give a competent technical opinion, who are you talking about? Who was the guy you were asking to do this? Is it the artillery commander or is it some other military commander you were talking to. Who were you asking for to provide that kind of support? Was it always the same person or who was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to 1999, in this area I mostly worked with one military command, and that was Colonel Mihajlo Gergar. I usually cooperated with him and when needed, I would ask him to provide assistance in the form of artillery support or some other fire support since the police did not have those weapons at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You made that distinction about 1999. Were there any occasions in 1998 where you requested artillery support?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: If I can give a you example. There were such situations. We came across a large barricade in a canyon on the road between Pec and Pristina. It was a large five-metre tall stone barrier. We couldn't break through it, and we asked for assistance because the area around it had been mind and since we will no means to break through that barricade we asked for assistance and the assistance was provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who did you make the request to on that occasion, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Commander Jankovic whom I mentioned. I think that was his last name. I think that he assisted me in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1998, other than this one with the big stone barrier in the road, did you ever request artillery support in connection with action or activity against KLA or terrorists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I did. We had situations where terrorists were firing at us with heavy machine-guns or recoilless guns or heavy hand-held rocket launchers. They had stone fences, and they would take a stone or a boulder out of that fence and make a hole through which they were shooting at police. It was very difficult for us to respond to that fire, and we didn't have the artillery, and that's why we asked for occasional assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall when and where any of those occasions were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I can remember a situation near Podujevo. Colonel Gergar described that in his statement, as did I. In 1998 on that road and along that road leading to Kijevo and Pristina, in several places they had prepared Molotov cocktails and barriers. They had mined the roads and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question now about that document we talked about before, 6D709. I think you have a hard copy there, and I think it's at the bottom of page 2 in the Serbian version, and in English it's page 3 under unit task it's item number 5.1. You were asked about this. We see a task for the 211th Armoured Brigade, parts of the brigade, with the 95th Military Territorial Detachment, and then it looks like in B/C/S it says 1 -- 1/122 MUP Intervention Brigade, and I think you said that was a company. That was one company of your Intervention Brigade? Is that what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. It says here one company, but one company wasn't enough so we took larger forces. Therefore, two companies were engaged and another unit, the JCO -- the JSO, which continued working further on. It says in the second line JSO is to put up a barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, earlier today when you talked about that you told us you thought that was a mistake there where it says JSO, because I think we saw an after action report where there was a reference to the SAJ. Do you recall now which is correct? Is it SAJ or is it JSO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: You're quite right. JSO is a mistake. It should say SAJ. I think that a mistake was made here in listing the tasks, and I think that SAJ was engaged in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And about how many men from your Intervention Brigade were engaged in this particular action, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that we got two companies involved in that area and that the SAJ, I don't know how many people they numbered, a company perhaps, and we didn't think that this action was dangerous enough to require stronger forces. We agreed with the army on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and what about the reference I see -- it looks like there's a reference right before JSO to OPG. Was there an OPG involved in this action separate and apart from the SAJ and the PJP detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have such a unit with such designation, OPG. I don't remember that any OPG was engaged in that area, if I remember correctly. Our forces were sufficient, plus the SAJ. We worked together with them. The only thing that there was is that I had guides from the Podujevo OUP who were familiar with the area, and there were just several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I remember you telling us about that. Could you look at the last page in the B/C/S. It's the last page in English as well. I think you told us you received this document; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: It seems familiar, the document, and I received it prior to the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One little question I have for you. You see at the very end there are two item numbers 14. I suppose that's a typographical error, but do you remember noticing that back in 1999 when you got the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC
utterances.text: See, this is not a police document, and it wasn't until today that I saw number 14 written here twice. I don't think it's deliberate. I suppose it's just a mistake, an honest mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is this a suitable time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is a good time, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zivaljevic, we will have to conclude our hearing for today at this time because there is another case here at 4.00. That means, regrettably, that we cannot complete your evidence and that you will have to return here on Tuesday when our next sitting is, and that's on Tuesday afternoon. That will be at 2.15 in this courtroom on Tuesday. Between now and then, it is extremely important that you have no communication with any person about the evidence in this case, and that means any aspect of the evidence. You can obviously communicate about any other matter, but not about the evidence. So could you please now leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 2.15 on Tuesday. We shall now go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of April, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
